title: Automation Bias and Deskilling in Radiology AI: A Confidence-stratified Triage Model for Workflow Integration.
desc: [Radiology. Artificial intelligence] Radiology is adopting artificial intelligence (AI) faster than it is studying what AI does to radiologists' perceptual expertise and interpretive skill. The question has partly shifted from whether these tools perform well on benchmark tasks to what happens to clinical judgment when use of these tools becomes routine. Two risks accompany this transition: automation bias, the tendency to follow AI suggestions without adequate scrutiny, and deskilling, the erosion of perceptual and interpretive ability through disuse, typically revealed when AI support is withdrawn. Incorrect AI output degrades accuracy regardless of experience, the benefit of assistance varies unpredictably across readers and tasks, and performance falls after AI withdrawal; neither risk has been studied longitudinally in radiology. A confidence-stratified triage model is proposed in which calibrated AI confidence, not findings alone, routes cases to low-, intermediate-, or high-confidence streams: output withheld until independent reading, shown with uncertainty signals and a checklist, or shown with random blinded audit. Demonstrated local confidence calibration is a precondition for deployment, and stream thresholds and audit rates should be weighted by task and potential clinical harm, not error probability alone. Rather than applying one workflow to every case, the model redistributes radiologist attention to where AI error is most likely and most consequential, operationalizing four principles: keeping the radiologist in the decision loop, making AI uncertainty visible, inserting targeted cognitive friction, and governing the human-AI interaction as a system. A research agenda to determine whether these countermeasures reduce automation bias and skill erosion in practice is also proposed.

title: Clinical Application of Artificial Intelligence in the Management of Chronic Hepatitis B.
source: PubMed · Journal of gastroenterology and hepatology
desc: [Journal of gastroenterology and hepatology] Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) burdens the healthcare system, affecting millions of individuals worldwide with a potential progression to complications such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The World Health Organization launched the chronic viral hepatitis elimination plan which aimed to eliminate chronic hepatitis B virus by 2030, yet the goal has seemed to be far from reach with the remaining few years owing to different hurdles ranging from screening strategy and diagnosis to risk stratification for antiviral treatment and HCC surveillance. To refine the management of CHB, previous studies focused on identifying the at-risk populations and predictors for adverse outcomes using conventional statistical methods. With the emerging role of artificial intelligence (AI), there is further room to improve different aspects of screening and management. For instance, generative AI, such as large language models (LLMs), has been proven to have the ability to answer different clinical questions, assisting patients' and physicians' decision on various clinical scenarios. Different machine learning and deep learning models have also been developed to assess for liver fibrosis, as well as to aid segmentation of liver structures and detection of focal liver lesions through various imaging modalities. While different AI models have shown superior performance compared to those developed through traditional statistical models, the lack of standardized datasets in training cohorts and the unresolved concerns of hallucination of false information in LLMs pose challenges on applying AI in the current management of CHB, in which further studies are required to adopt AI into daily clinical practice.

title: AI-Assisted Differentiation of Autoimmune Pancreatitis and Pancreatic Cancer Using EUS: A Multicenter Ambispective Study
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Ruijin Hospital; conditions: Autoimmune Pancreatitis, Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC); type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 690; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Focal autoimmune pancreatitis (f-AIP) and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) exhibit substantial overlap in clinical manifestations and imaging features, posing a major diagnostic challenge in pancreatic diseases. Given the marked differences in treatment strategies and prognosis, accurate differentiation is essential to avoid unnecessary surgery and ensure timely initiation of anticancer treatment. This study aims to collect endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) images from patients with confirmed f-AIP or PDAC across multiple centers, using a previously established multicenter database. Data collected before January 2026 will be used to develop an artificial intelligence (AI) model based on EUS radiomics for differential diagnosis. Subsequently, prospectively collected data from participating centers from 2026 onward will be used for model testing and validation. The diagnostic performance of the model will be evaluated and compared with that of endoscopists with different levels of experience. Furthermore, this study will investigate the clinical value of interpretable radiomic features, with particular emphasis on challenging diagnostic scenarios, including IgG4-negative AIP, AIP with elevated carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) levels, and PDAC with imaging features resembling those of AIP. The ultimate goal is to provide a reliable tool for accurate, noninvasive preoperative differential diagnosis while promoting the standardization of multicenter AIP databases and the sharing and utilization of imaging data resources.

title: MoveBench: A Rubric-Based Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Sports and Health Coaching
desc: Despite rapid advances in large language models (LLMs), their deployment in the sports and health domain remains high-risk due to the absence of domain-specific evaluation benchmarks. Existing general-purpose benchmarks (e.g., MMLU and HELM) primarily assess broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities, but fail to capture critical domain requirements such as exercise safety, physiological appropriateness, personalization, and actionable coaching quality. This gap is particularly concerning in fitness and health applications, where incorrect or unsafe recommendations can lead to physical harm. To address this limitation, we introduce MoveBench, the first comprehensive benchmarking framework specifically designed for evaluating LLMs in sports and health coaching. The proposed benchmark integrates heterogeneous task formats, including multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and open-ended question answering (OpenQA), grounded in real-world user scenarios and paired with structured rubrics emphasizing safety compliance, scientific validity, and training logic. Through large-scale evaluation of 15 diverse LLMs on 809 questions with 5,012 rubric-level criteria, our results reveal substantial performance variability, particularly in safety awareness, structured program design, and personalization capability, highlighting a critical gap between knowing and doing. Our work establishes a foundational evaluation standard for sports and health LLM applications and provides a reproducible framework for advancing safe, reliable, and context-aware AI-driven coaching systems. Open resources are available at https://github.com/SatoSakula/MoveBench.

title: Richer database context improves LLM-generated EHR phenotyping algorithms
desc: Objective: To evaluate large language model (LLM) generation of type 2 diabetes (T2DM) phenotyping SQL and the effect of database implementation context. Materials and Methods: Eight publicly accessible LLM-based systems generated SQL under progressively richer prompts using synthetic and University of North Carolina (UNC) Health electronic health record (EHR) data, both based on the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) model. Outputs were compared with the Electronic Medical Records and Genomics (eMERGE) T2DM reference phenotype using SQL executability, F1, positive predictive value (PPV), and recall. Results: Fewer than 55% of limited-context synthetic outputs and no limited-context UNC EHR outputs executed without modification. Detailed codebooks (L3) increased executability to 81.3% in synthetic OMOP and 100% in UNC EHR; adding sample rows (L4) increased synthetic executability to 100%. Limited-context recall was as low as 0.01, whereas high-context outputs achieved recall [≥]0.99 at synthetic L4 and >0.90 at UNC L3, although UNC PPV remained substantially lower than recall. At the highest available context levels, Beta F1 ranged from 0.72-0.99 in synthetic OMOP and 0.57-0.68 in UNC EHR; all UNC models exceeded the diagnosis-code baseline (F1=0.54). The top synthetic performer fell from F1=0.99 to 0.64 on UNC EHR. Discussion: Richer database context was associated with more consistent SQL executability and recall, while model rankings varied across datasets. Conclusion: LLMs can generate clinically meaningful T2DM phenotyping SQL when provided with sufficient database context, but limited PPV in real-world data underscores the need for local validation.

title: M4Bench: Evaluating Procedural Specification for Clinical EHR Derivation Agents
desc: Clinical research over electronic health records depends on derived variables whose definitions sit outside the schema, in item codes, time windows, missingness rules, and output-grain choices that change cohorts and downstream conclusions. We introduce M4Bench, 28 clinical derivation tasks across 15 task families on MIMIC-IV and eICU, to test whether AI coding agents can reproduce such derivations and how clinician-reviewed agent skills change their results. Its controls decompose the value of skills into specification completeness, delivery format, and schema familiarity. In a Docker-isolated Codex campaign (GPT 5.4 Mini and GPT 5.5), skills raise reward by 0.136 over the no-skill baseline, with 26 of 28 tasks improving. Specification completeness accounts for most of this gain: on an eight-task control subset, an operational spec alone raises reward by 0.162, and skills add only 0.024 on top, indistinguishable from zero. On a ten-task subset, decoy skills score like no skill and raw reference SQL nearly matches targeted skills, arguing against generic context or the skill format as the explanation. Schema obfuscation and restructuring preserve 86% and 70% of the skill gain (GPT 5.4 Mini, 26 MIMIC-IV tasks), a descriptive robustness check rather than a bound on memorization. A descriptive Claude Code replication on all 28 tasks (Opus 4.7 and Sonnet 4.6, 560 runs) is directionally consistent (+0.120, 21 of 28 tasks improving). These gains are partial agreement with the reference, not completed tasks: only 25 of 280 with-skill and 13 of 280 no-skill Codex runs pass every strict check, and skills barely change which rows agents return (key F1 +0.003). Skills are released as a versioned, clinician-reviewable markdown delivery format, with a family-level reference-validity audit. M4Bench releases tasks, skills, evaluation code, and sanitized per-run evidence as an open-source benchmark.

title: Xenograft supervision and joint methylation-fragment-end encoding define a reusable molecular scoring layer for cell-free tumor DNA
desc: Circulating tumor DNA is often scarce in plasma, and regional methylation summaries can obscure informative differences between individual molecules. Here we present ctDNA-BERT, a Transformer that scores individual bisulfite reads without predefined differentially methylated regions by jointly encoding CpG methylation state, nucleotide context and the fragment 3' end. Xenografts provide molecule-level tumor supervision. The resulting frozen scorer supported tumor-fraction estimation in synthetic and patient-derived xenograft mixtures and enriched tumor-concordant methylation and chromatin-accessibility signals in independent hepatocellular carcinoma and stage III pan-cancer plasma without cohort-specific retraining. Features derived from selected reads discriminated stage I cancers from healthy controls in a retrospective cohort of 1,477 specimens, achieving an out-of-fold area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.884. By separating molecular scoring from sample-level inference, ctDNA-BERT provides a reusable read-level scoring layer for cell-free DNA methylation analysis.
